PUBLIC COMMENT

The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal
Code. If you wish to address City Council, please complete a speaker card and hand the card to the Sergeant
at Arms. City Council will hear public comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and
prior to a vote and on matters not listed on the agenda during the Public Comment period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or
unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or
schedule certain matters for consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council: Comments are limited to 3 minutes
or less and should be directed to City Council as a whole. Individuals are not permitted to extend, transfer, speak
on behalf of others, or yield their time to other speakers. Please refrain from any disruptive conduct.

  SEPTEMBER 1, 2026

  CLOSED SESSION MEETING

Mayor Perez called the meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk
City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call were
Councilmembers Ayala and Ramirez, and Mayor Perez. Vice Mayor Rios arrived after
roll call and Councilmember Valencia was absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez,
City Manager; Arnold M. Alvarez-Glasman, City Attorney; and Theresa Devoy, City Clerk.

ORAL COMMUNICATIONS FOR CLOSED SESSION MATTERS

There were no persons wishing to address City Council on the matters to be discussed
in closed session.

CLOSED SESSION

City Council immediately convened to closed session for discussion on the following
matters:

  I. CONFERENCE WITH LEGAL COUNSEL – EXISTING LITIGATION PURSUANT
  TO GOVERNMENT CODE §54956.9(d)(1) – West Coast Arborists, Inc. vs. City of
  Norwalk, et al. Los Angeles Superior Court Case No. 26STCP03027.

  II. CONFERENCE WITH LABOR NEGOTIATOR PURSUANT TO GOVERNMENT
  CODE §54957.6: Agency Representative: City Council; Unrepresented Employee-
  City Manager.

RECESS

City Council recessed at 6:18 p.m. pending the commencement of the regular meeting.

  REGULAR MEETING

Mayor Perez called the meeting to order at 6:22 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk
City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call were
Councilmembers Ayala and Ramirez, Vice Mayor Rios, and Mayor Perez.
Councilmember Valencia was absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez, City
Manager; Arnold M. Alvarez-Glasman, City Attorney; and Theresa Devoy, City Clerk.

The invocation was delivered by Pastor Michael Gutierrez, Redeemer Covenant Church;
followed by the flag salute, led by Dominic Ortiz Olivas, Earl E. Edmondson Elementary
School.

Norwalk City Council
September 1, 2026

CLOSED SESSION REPORT

The City Attorney indicated there was no reportable action taken on the matters discussed
in closed session.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

Councilmember Ayala wished his wife a Happy 42nd Anniversary. Vice Mayor Rios
reported on her attendance at the William Orr Elementary School Ribbon Cutting event;
invited all to attend the Lattes and Leashes events held every Saturday in September at
Bob White Park; highlighted the upcoming Shanti Glow Ribbon Cutting event September
5, at 11005 Firestone Boulevard; and encouraged all to practice safe driving. Mayor
Perez shared that the City newsletters were distributed including the Norwalk Now
featuring “Build Up Norwalk” highlighting exciting developments taking place in the City;
announced Senior Center Month, sharing the excellent service staff has provided
throughout the year; congratulated Norwalk Transportation on their win at the Bus Rodeo;
and reported on her attendance at the California Contract Cities Board of Directors
Meeting, Neighborhood Watch Meetings, the Joint Powers Insurance Authority Claims
and Executive Committee Meeting, and the California Contract Cities Association Fall
Educational Summit with Vice Mayor Rios and Councilmember Ramirez.

SPECIAL PRESENTATIONS

City Council proclaimed September as the Norwalk Housing Authority’s 50th Anniversary
Month with the Housing Division accepting the proclamation.

City Council proclaimed September as National Preparedness Month in the City with the
Public Safety Department accepting the proclamation. Rita Ruiz, Director of Public Safety
announced that the City will be participating in an Active Shooter Training, September 4.

City Council proclaimed September as Senior Center Month in the City, with Gabriela
Regalado, Director of Social Services highlighting their accomplishments, and Senior
Center staff accepting the proclamation.

CITY MANAGER COMMENTS

Levy Sun, Communications Director, shared a Traffic Safety Incident statement. Mr.
Gomez announced that a Strategic Plan Special Meeting will be held on October 24, at
10:30 a.m. Mr. Gomez shared resources available to residents for those impacted by
Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Videos were shared highlighting El Nino
preparedness, 2026 Back-to-School safety, and the “Bi-Weekly Review”.

SUBJECT: AGREEMENT AMENDMENT NO. 2 FOR INSTALLATION OF SECURITY
  BADGE READERS AT CITYWIDE FACILITIES

Background:

In May 2026, City Council approved an agreement with ASSI Security (“ASSI”) for services
related to the installation of security badge readers at Citywide facilities to increase access
control and safety for residents, visitors, and staff. Since its implementation, staff and ASSI have
coordinated and successfully completed the first phase of this project. A total of 24 doors at City
Hall now require security card access to enter restricted areas within the building. These
restricted areas of access are specific to each person assigned an employee badge. Also
included at City Hall was the installation of a video intercom system and a master station at the
front reception with door release, which was executed via the First Amendment.

The next phase of this project will be the installation of badge readers at the Transportation
Center and Public Services Department. After a walkthrough of the facility, staff determined that
there are 14 doors that require installation of security badge readers. Also included in the scope
of work for this Second Amendment is the installation of card readers on City owned property,
specifically a freight elevator and the purchase of HID Mobile Credentials, which will allow
vendors authorized access to City facilities through Bluetooth. This will allow staff to grant and
disable any access to facilities without needing to issue physical key cards.

Access control of all City facilities continues to remain a priority for City staff. Security badge
readers secure entry and exit points, by allowing all authorized and unauthorized access to be
monitored through logs. ASSI continues to demonstrate technical expertise in the installation of
security badge readers while also understanding the City’s operational needs and requirements.

The anticipated fiscal impact of the proposed work for this Second Amendment is $73,460.

and authorize the City Manager to execute the agreement and any amendments, provided there
is funding in the budget and it is within the City Manager’s signing authority, on behalf of the City,
in a form approved by the City Attorney.

  SUBJECT: RESOLUTION NO. 26-57 - RESTRUCTURE THE YOUTH COMMISSION AS A
  YOUTH ADVISORY BOARD AND ESTABLISH PROCEDURES

  Background:

  In March 2021, City Council adopted Resolution No. 21-15, which amended Resolution No. 20-
  61: the Advisory Body Procedure resolution to re-establish the Norwalk Youth Commission. Past
  criteria for participation included 1) Students within 13-18 years of age; 2) Students living in
  Norwalk who are currently in high school or recently graduated from various grade levels and
  schools; 3) Selection of up to 15 members, with each Councilmember appointing 3
  representatives each; and 4) Each members would have two year terms.

  While the Youth Commission was active, staff faced ongoing challenges such as
  Commissioner absences, low retention, and lack of participation. Commissioners were regularly
  removed from the Commission due to missed meetings, while others left before completing their
  full terms. Additionally, some commissioners demonstrated limited engagement or involvement
  as a result of conflicting extracurricular commitments. Due to these challenges, staff
  recommended the Youth Commission be restructured as a Youth Advisory Board.

  On August 4, 2026, the Recreation and Park Services Department (RPSD) proposed the
  Norwalk Youth Advisory Board. The board will provide guidance and recommendations to the
  Norwalk City Council and the Recreation and Park Services Department in the following areas:

1. Teen Alliance Program (T.A.P.)
  2. Youth leadership
  3. Teen Center operations and programs
  4. Youth & Government education & engagement
  5. City events and programs related to youth development
 City Council  September 15, 2026
Resolution No. 26-57 – Restructuring the Youth Commission  Page No. 2
as a Youth Advisory Board and Establishing Procedures

The new advisory board format would consist of the following:

  1. Ten members
  2. Members must be between the ages of 13 and 18
  3. Members must be a resident of the City of Norwalk
  4. Members must attend a middle school or high school in a public school district, private
  institution, or home school that serves Norwalk residents.
  5. Members will serve a two-year term from January 1 - December 31 (aligning with all
  other City Advisory Bodies)
  6. It is preferred (not required) that members complete 50 hours of volunteer service in
  T.A.P.

APPLICATION REQUIREMENTS
The following would be required to participate as a Youth Advisory Board Member:

  1. Complete the online application (If under 18, a parent or legal guardian must also sign
  the parental consent form)
  2. Provide two letters of recommendation (one personal/one professional)
  3. If selected, participate in an in-person interview with RPSD staff.
  4. The list of qualifying candidates (up to 20) will be shared with City Council members to
  make final selections. Each Councilmember will select two candidates for
  representation on the Youth Advisory Board.

APPLICATION DEADLINE AND TIMELINE
  1. September 21 - October 20 | Marketing Period
  2. October 1 - 20 | Application Period
  3. October 21 - 31 | Application Review
  4. November 2 - 6 | Applicant interviews
  5. November 9 - 13 | Qualified List reviewed by City Council
  6. December 15 | Appointments by City Council
  7. January 4 - 22, 2027 | Onboarding process
  8. January 27, 2027 | 1st Meeting of Youth Advisory Board
  9. January 1, 2027 - December 31, 2029 | Two-Year Advisory Body Term

ATTENDANCE GUIDELINES
To assist with retention and participation, new attendance guidelines would be as follows:

  1. Up to two excused absences:
  a. Sickness (with doctor’s note)
  b. Medical/Dental Appointment (with doctor’s note)
  c. Family Emergency (with parental note)
  d. Sport Game/Tournament (with parental or school note)
  2. Up to two unexcused absences. Participants will be removed from the board if they have
  more than two unexcused absences. Exceptions will be made for extended illness with
  doctor’s note.
 City Council  September 15, 2026
Resolution No. 26-57 – Restructuring the Youth Commission  Page No. 3
as a Youth Advisory Board and Establishing Procedures

  3. Meeting quorum is unchanged at a majority of those appointed to any Advisory Body.

Excused and unexcused absences will be accounted for annually during the two-year term.

Furthermore, the proposed transition from a Youth Commission to a Youth Advisory Board will
strengthen youth engagement by providing meaningful input and direction on City programs,
services, and initiatives while offering greater flexibility in participation. Less restrictive guidelines
will help accommodate teens’ academic and extracurricular commitments, supporting sustained
engagement and longer-term retention. The Youth Advisory Board would also provide valuable
leadership opportunities and empower Norwalk youth to help advance initiatives that reflect their
needs and interests.

  AGREEMENT AMENDMENT FOR ON-CALL COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
  AND ADDITIONAL SERVICES FOR THE NORWALK TRANSIT VILLAGE

Background:

In December 2024, an Agreement of Purchase and Sale and Initial Escrow Instruction was
entered into by the City and State of California (“State”) through its Department of General
Services for the former California Youth Authority. The site is comprised of approximately 32
acres together with improvements of approximately 35-40 structures and ancillary improvements
located at 13200 Bloomfield Avenue (“Property”). Escrow closed on July 28, 2025, for the surplus
Property pursuant to the provisions of California Assembly Bill No. 518, Chapter 43, Statutes of
2020. The project will create a Transit Oriented Development within the City’s Economic
Development Node No. 6.

On November 7, 2023, City Council approved agreements with 27 firms to provide on-call
Community Development Consultant and Additional Services (Services). As part of the
approvals, Michael Baker International, Inc. (MBI) was awarded a contract to continue providing
on-call Community Development Consultant and Additional Service to the City. MBI worked on
the environmental analysis to ensure that the entire California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
process was conducted in a comprehensive manner and concurrently with the entitlements for
the Norwalk Transit Village (Project). MBI has submitted a proposal for CEQA consulting
services associated with subsequent approvals for the Project. The scope of work is to prepare
an Addendum for the 2024 Certified Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the purpose of CEQA
compliance. MBI will prepare the technical studies: transportation (including updated trip
generation calculations and Vehicle Miles Traveled screening assessment), air quality,
 City Council  September 15, 2026

greenhouse gas emissions, energy, and noise studies, as well as an update to the Water
Demand Calculations and an optional task for an update to the Water Supply Assessment. The
MBI work for the Addendum is not-to-exceed $85,000 and is within the current $200,000 contract
compensation amount.

CSG Consultants, Inc. (CSG) was also awarded a contract in November 2023 to provide on-call
Community Development Consultant and Additional Services with compensation not-to-exceed
$150,000 annually. CSG’s Amendment No. 1 was approved in May 2026 to increase the
compensation to not-to-exceed $606,400 and extend the term related to the Project
Management Services for the Norwalk Transit Village and Building Inspection Services for The
Walk. CSG is assigned to assist with Project Management Services for the Project. CSG’s staff
helped with site design, community outreach activities, entitlement processing and public
hearings for the Project. The current services include continued efforts to remediate the site and
complete the land transfer process. Amendment No. 2 is for continued Project Management
Servies and the work related to the Specific Plan Amendment consisting of the following tasks
not to exceed $110,000:

•  Task 1 – Continued Project Management

•  Task 2 – Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan Amendment

•  Task 3 – Specific Plan Review, Public Hearings and Adoption

Furthermore, the contracts with MBI and CSG have provided staff augmentation services for the
Building and Planning Divisions. The continued need for on-call professional services are
necessary in order to maintain service levels during staff changes, provide expedited entitlement
processing for priority projects, and maintain service levels during temporary increase in activity.
Additional funds are also needed to continue work with the Department of Toxic Substances
Control for the remediation activities and the land transfer process. The next phase of the Project
is the demolition and remediation work.

Fiscal Impact:

Additional funding for the Project will come from the former Redevelopment Non-Housing bond
proceeds in the amount of $195,000.

Funding for the Project expenses related to remediation activities shall be reimbursed to the City
from State funds currently held in Escrow for such purposes.
